title: Trump Cancels $1 Billion in Spending — Without Asking Congress First
summary:
Imagine saving up your allowance for something important — and then someone else decides to spend it on something totally different. That's kind of what's happening in Washington right now.

On Friday, President Donald Trump announced he is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending that Congress already approved. Most of the cuts hit programs that help refugees and kids who came to the U.S. without permission. The White House says the money isn't needed anymore because fewer people are crossing the border illegally.

Other programs on the chopping block: a school program for migrant students, an office that works to reduce racial tension, and a program that helps minority business owners.

But here's the twist — even some Republicans are upset. Senator Susan Collins of Maine, who leads the Senate committee that handles spending, said she got no warning. She called it a "usurpation" (that means taking power that isn't yours) of Congress's job to decide how money gets spent.

Under the rules, Congress gets 45 days to review cuts like these. Trump announced them with only five days left — and the House is out of session. The Government Accountability Office says this move is illegal. So who really decides? That fight is just getting started.
why_it_matters: This fight is about who gets to decide how the country's money is used — and that money pays for things kids see every day, like school programs and help for families in need.

background_read: Congress is the part of the U.S. government that decides how the country's tax money is spent. The Constitution gives Congress this 'power of the purse', so presidents normally cannot refuse to spend money that lawmakers have already approved.
The Government Accountability Office (a government office that acts like a watchdog, checking how money is spent) says this move breaks the rules.
In the 1970s, a president tried to block spending he disagreed with, so Congress passed a law saying lawmakers must get 45 days to review cuts like these.
Article_Structure: WHO: President Donald Trump (the U.S. president since 2025), Senator Susan Collins of Maine (she leads the Senate committee that handles spending), the Government Accountability Office, and Congress.

WHAT: Trump announced he is canceling nearly $1 billion that Congress already approved, mostly from programs helping refugees and kids who came to the U.S. without permission; the Government Accountability Office says the move is illegal.
WHERE: Washington, D.C., where the White House, the Senate, and the House of Representatives all work.

WHY: The White House says fewer people are crossing the border illegally, so the money isn't needed — but critics say deciding how money is spent is Congress's job, not the president's, and the House is out of session with only five of the 45 review days left.

perspectives.description: It says the money is no longer needed because fewer people are crossing the border illegally, so cutting it saves money that would otherwise be wasted.
Senator Susan Collins said she got no warning and called it a 'usurpation' of Congress's job, while the Government Accountability Office says the move is illegal.
A school program for migrant students, an office that works to reduce racial tension, and a program that helps minority business owners could lose their funding.
Because Congress gets 45 days to review cuts and only five were left, the argument over who really decides may end up in a longer political or legal fight.
